narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 18, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your first-year law school grades came next; being in the 7th decile (above the accepted students’ average of 6th) worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA ranked third. At 2.7 versus an accepted average of 3.23, it also nudged the outcome toward failure, though less forcefully than your LSAT.

Taken together, the low LSAT and below-average college grades outweighed the positive signal from your stronger first-year performance in law school, resulting in the rejection.

You should focus on improving your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as it carries the greatest weight. Retaking the test and raising that score could substantially improve your chances on a future application. Consider also strengthening your undergraduate record narrative or adding other evidence of academic growth before reapplying.
